Example—auxin: Darwin and later Went contributed to its discovery; produced in shoot tips/young tissues; promotes cell elongation, apical dominance, root initiation, tropic responses and fruit development. Uses include rooting powders, prevention of premature fruit drop and selective weed control (synthetic auxins).

questions.text: What do you understand by photoperiodism and vernalisation? Describe their significance.
questions.answer: Photoperiodism is the response of plants to relative lengths of day and night, especially flowering. Vernalisation is promotion of flowering by exposure to low temperature. Both help plants flower in suitable seasons and synchronise reproduction with favourable conditions.

questions.text: Why is abscisic acid also known as stress hormone?
questions.answer: Abscisic acid promotes responses to stress, especially drought: it induces stomatal closure, inhibits growth, promotes seed/bud dormancy and helps plants tolerate unfavourable conditions; hence it is called the stress hormone.

questions.text: ‘Both growth and differentiation in higher plants are open’. Comment.
questions.answer: Growth is open because meristems remain active and can produce new cells throughout life. Differentiation is also open/plastic because cells can retain or regain developmental potential and may differentiate differently depending on position and environment.

questions.text: ‘Both a short day plant and a long day plant can produce can flower simultaneously in a given place’. Explain.
questions.answer: Yes. Flowering depends on each species' critical photoperiod and, importantly, the length of uninterrupted night. At a particular place and season, day/night duration may fall within the inductive range of both a short-day and a long-day plant if their critical thresholds differ.

questions.text: Which one of the plant growth regulators would you use if you are asked to: (a) induce rooting in a twig (b) quickly ripen a fruit (c) delay leaf senescence (d) induce growth in axillary buds (e) ‘bolt’ a rosette plant (f) induce immediate stomatal closure in leaves.
questions.answer: (a) Auxin (e.g. IBA/NAA) (b) Ethylene (often applied as ethephon) (c) Cytokinin (d) Cytokinin (e) Gibberellin (GA3) (f) Abscisic acid (ABA).

questions.text: Would a defoliated plant respond to photoperiodic cycle? Why?
questions.answer: Usually no, because leaves perceive photoperiod and produce a flowering stimulus (florigen) that is transported to the shoot apex. A completely defoliated plant lacks the main photoperiod-perceiving organs, so it generally does not respond normally.

questions.text: What would be expected to happen if: (a) GA3 is applied to rice seedlings (b) dividing cells stop differentiating (c) a rotten fruit gets mixed with unripe fruits (d) you forget to add cytokinin to the culture medium.
questions.answer: (a) GA3 promotes internode elongation and may cause excessive stem elongation/bolting in rice seedlings. (b) Dividing cells that do not differentiate may form an undifferentiated mass of cells. (c) Ethylene released by the rotten fruit accelerates ripening of nearby unripe fruits. (d) Without cytokinin, cell division and shoot formation in tissue culture are reduced; auxin-dominant conditions may favour roots or callus rather than shoots.

questions.text: Choose the correct answer among the following : (a) Gastric juice contains (i) pepsin, lipase and rennin (ii) trypsin, lipase and rennin (iii) trypsin, pepsin and lipase (iv) trypsin, pepsin and renin (b) Succus entericus is the name given to (i) a junction between ileum and large intestine (ii) intestinal juice (iii) swelling in the gut (iv) appendix
questions.answer: (a) (i) pepsin, lipase and rennin is the best answer among the listed options (rennin is mainly important in infants; gastric juice contains pepsin and gastric lipase). (b) (ii) intestinal juice.

questions.text: Match column I with column II Column I Column II (a) Bilirubin and biliverdin (i) Parotid (b) Hydrolysis of starch (ii) Bile (c) Digestion of fat (iii) Lipases (d) Salivary gland (iv) Amylases
questions.answer: (a) Bilirubin and biliverdin – (ii) bile; (b) Hydrolysis of starch – (iv) amylases; (c) Digestion of fat – (iii) lipases; (d) Salivary gland – (i) parotid.

questions.text: Answer briefly: (a) Why are villi present in the intestine and not in the stomach? (b) How does pepsinogen change into its active form? (c) What are the basic layers of the wall of alimentary canal? (d) How does bile help in the digestion of fats?
questions.answer: (a) Villi greatly increase the surface area for absorption of digested nutrients; the stomach is mainly for storage, mixing and initial protein digestion and does not need villi. (b) HCl in gastric juice converts inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin; pepsin then activates more pepsinogen. (c) Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa. (d) Bile salts emulsify fats into small droplets and aid lipase action and micelle formation; bile also helps neutralise acidic chyme.

questions.text: State the role of pancreatic juice in digestion of proteins.
questions.answer: Pancreatic juice contains proteases secreted as inactive zymogens: trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase/enteropeptidase to trypsin; trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidases. These enzymes break proteins and peptides into smaller peptides and amino acids.

questions.text: Describe the process of digestion of protein in stomach.
questions.answer: In the stomach, HCl denatures proteins and provides an acidic pH; it converts pepsinogen to pepsin. Pepsin breaks proteins into smaller peptides and proteoses/peptones. In infants, rennin helps coagulate milk protein.

questions.text: Give the dental formula of human beings.
questions.answer: Adult human dental formula: 2.1.2.3 / 2.1.2.3 = 32 teeth (per half of each jaw: 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars, 3 molars).

questions.text: Bile juice contains no digestive enzymes, yet it is important for digestion. Why?
questions.answer: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for pancreatic lipase. They also help form micelles for absorption of fatty acids and monoglycerides; bile is alkaline and helps neutralise acidic chyme.

questions.text: Describe the digestive role of chymotrypsin. Which two other digestive enzymes of the same category are secreted by its source gland?
questions.answer: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic protease that hydrolyses peptide bonds, especially near aromatic amino acids. It is secreted as chymotrypsinogen and activated by trypsin. The other pancreatic proteases in the same group include trypsin and carboxypeptidase.

questions.text: How are polysaccharides and disaccharides digested?
questions.answer: Polysaccharides are hydrolysed by amylases into smaller oligosaccharides/disaccharides. Brush-border enzymes then digest disaccharides: maltase → glucose, sucrase → glucose + fructose, lactase → glucose + galactose. Monosaccharides are absorbed through intestinal epithelium.

questions.text: What would happen if HCl were not secreted in the stomach?
questions.answer: Without HCl, the stomach would not maintain the acidic pH needed for pepsin activation and action; protein digestion would be impaired, and the antimicrobial action of gastric juice would decrease.

questions.text: How does butter in your food get digested and absorbed in the body?
questions.answer: Butter fat is emulsified by bile salts in the small intestine. Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses triglycerides mainly into monoglycerides and fatty acids. These form micelles, enter intestinal epithelial cells, are re-esterified to triglycerides and packaged into chylomicrons, which enter lacteals and then lymph before reaching blood.

questions.text: Discuss the main steps in the digestion of proteins as the food passes through different parts of the alimentary canal.
questions.answer: In the stomach, HCl denatures proteins and activates pepsin, which forms smaller peptides. In the small intestine, pancreatic proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidases) further hydrolyse peptides. Brush-border peptidases produce amino acids and small peptides, which are absorbed into intestinal cells and pass into blood.

questions.text: Explain the term thecodont and diphyodont.
questions.answer: Thecodont dentition means teeth are embedded in sockets of the jaw bones. Diphyodont dentition means two successive sets of teeth occur during life: deciduous (milk) teeth and permanent teeth.

questions.text: Name different types of teeth and their number in an adult human.
questions.answer: Adult humans have 32 teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars.

questions.text: What are the functions of liver?
questions.answer: The liver produces bile; regulates carbohydrate, lipid and protein metabolism; stores glycogen, vitamins and iron; deaminates amino acids and forms urea; detoxifies drugs/toxins; synthesises plasma proteins and clotting factors; and breaks down old RBCs/haemoglobin.

questions.text: Define vital capacity. What is its significance?
questions.answer: Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a maximum inspiration. It equals IRV + tidal volume + ERV and indicates the usable ventilatory capacity of the lungs and respiratory muscles.

questions.text: State the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal breathing.
questions.answer: After a normal expiration, the air remaining in the lungs is the functional residual capacity (FRC), approximately 2,300 mL in a typical adult.

questions.text: Diffusion of gases occurs in the alveolar region only and not in the other parts of respiratory system. Why?
questions.answer: Alveoli have an extremely thin respiratory membrane, extensive surface area, dense capillary network and moist lining, providing a short diffusion distance. Other respiratory passages mainly conduct, warm, filter and humidify air and lack this specialised exchange surface.

questions.text: What are the major transport mechanisms for CO2? Explain.
questions.answer: About 7% of CO2 is transported dissolved in plasma, about 20–25% bound to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin, and about 70% as bicarbonate ions. In RBCs, carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 and water to carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3−; bicarbonate moves into plasma in exchange for chloride.

questions.text: What will be the pO2 and pCO2 in the atmospheric air compared to those in the alveolar air ? (i) pO2 lesser, pCO2 higher (ii) pO2 higher, pCO2 lesser (iii) pO2 higher, pCO2 higher (iv) pO2 lesser, pCO2 lesser
questions.answer: (ii) Atmospheric air has higher pO2 and lower pCO2 than alveolar air.

questions.text: Explain the process of inspiration under normal conditions.
questions.answer: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and external intercostal muscles raise the ribs and sternum. Thoracic volume increases, intrapulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, and air flows into the lungs.

questions.text: How is respiration regulated?
questions.answer: Respiration is regulated by respiratory centres in the medulla oblongata and pons. Chemosensitive areas respond mainly to CO2/H+ changes; peripheral receptors in carotid and aortic bodies detect changes in blood gases, especially low O2, and influence ventilation.

questions.text: What is the effect of pCO2 on oxygen transport?
questions.answer: An increase in pCO2 lowers blood pH and promotes oxygen unloading from haemoglobin (Bohr effect), shifting the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. This enhances oxygen delivery to metabolically active tissues.

questions.text: What happens to the respiratory process in a man going up a hill?
questions.answer: At high altitude, atmospheric and alveolar pO2 fall, so less oxygen diffuses into blood. Breathing rate and depth increase; over time, acclimatisation includes increased RBC production and other adjustments. Severe oxygen shortage can cause altitude sickness.

questions.text: What is the site of gaseous exchange in an insect?
questions.answer: In insects, gaseous exchange occurs through the tracheal system: air enters spiracles, passes through tracheae and fine tracheoles, and diffuses directly to/from tissues.

questions.text: Define oxygen dissociation curve. Can you suggest any reason for its sigmoidal pattern?
questions.answer: The oxygen dissociation curve shows the relationship between pO2 and percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen. Its sigmoid shape results from cooperative binding: binding of one O2 molecule increases haemoglobin's affinity for the next O2 molecules.

questions.text: Have you heard about hypoxia? Try to gather information about it, and discuss with your friends.
questions.answer: Hypoxia is inadequate oxygen availability at tissue level. It may result from low environmental oxygen, impaired lung gas exchange, reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood or poor circulation. Symptoms and causes depend on type and severity; severe cases require urgent medical assessment.

questions.text: Distinguish between (a) IRV and ERV (b) Inspiratory capacity and Expiratory capacity. (c) Vital capacity and Total lung capacity.
questions.answer: (a) IRV is the extra air forcibly inhaled after normal inspiration; ERV is the extra air forcibly exhaled after normal expiration. (b) Inspiratory capacity = tidal volume + IRV; expiratory capacity = tidal volume + ERV. (c) Vital capacity = IRV + TV + ERV; total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume.

questions.text: What is Tidal volume? Find out the Tidal volume (approximate value) for a healthy human in an hour.
questions.answer: Tidal volume is the air inspired or expired during a normal quiet breath, about 500 mL in a typical adult. At 12 breaths/min, minute ventilation is about 6 L/min; over one hour, about 360 L of air is moved (500 mL × 12 × 60), assuming a constant rate.

questions.text: Name the components of the formed elements in the blood and mention one major function of each of them.
questions.answer: Formed elements: RBCs transport oxygen (and some CO2); WBCs defend against infection; platelets help blood clotting.

questions.text: What is the importance of plasma proteins?
questions.answer: Albumins maintain colloid osmotic pressure and help maintain blood volume; globulins include antibodies and transport proteins; fibrinogen is essential for clotting. Plasma proteins also buffer pH and transport substances.

questions.text: Match Column I with Column II : Column I Column II (a) Eosinophils (i) Coagulation (b) RBC (ii) Universal Recipient (c) AB Group (iii) Resist Infections (d) Platelets (iv) Contraction of Heart (e) Systole (v) Gas transport
questions.answer: (a) Eosinophils – (iii) resist infections (especially parasites/allergic responses); (b) RBC – (v) gas transport; (c) AB group – (ii) universal recipient for red-cell transfusion in the ABO system (with Rh compatibility considered); (d) Platelets – (i) coagulation; (e) Systole – (iv) contraction of heart (the supplied match wording is imprecise; systole is contraction, not the heart itself).

questions.text: Why do we consider blood as a connective tissue?
questions.answer: Blood is a connective tissue because it has cells/cell fragments suspended in an extracellular matrix (plasma), transports materials between tissues and has a common mesodermal origin.

questions.text: What is the difference between lymph and blood?
questions.answer: Blood is a red fluid connective tissue with RBCs, WBCs and platelets suspended in plasma; it transports gases, nutrients, wastes and hormones. Lymph is a clear tissue fluid in lymphatic vessels, usually lacks RBCs and has fewer proteins; it returns tissue fluid to blood, transports absorbed fats and supports immunity.

questions.text: What is meant by double circulation? What is its significance?
questions.answer: Double circulation means blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit: pulmonary circulation (heart–lungs–heart) and systemic circulation (heart–body–heart). It keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate and supports efficient oxygen delivery at high metabolic rates.

questions.text: Write the differences between : (a) Blood and Lymph (b) Open and Closed system of circulation (c) Systole and Diastole (d) P-wave and T-wave
questions.answer: (a) Blood contains RBCs, WBCs and platelets in plasma; lymph is tissue fluid in lymph vessels, usually without RBCs and with lower protein. (b) Open circulation: fluid leaves vessels and bathes organs in sinuses; closed circulation: blood remains in vessels. (c) Systole is contraction; diastole is relaxation/filling. (d) ECG P wave represents atrial depolarisation; T wave represents ventricular repolarisation.

questions.text: Describe the evolutionary change in the pattern of heart among the vertebrates.
questions.answer: Fishes generally have a two-chambered heart and single circulation. Amphibians and most reptiles have a three-chambered heart with incomplete separation and some mixing (crocodilians have four chambers). Birds and mammals have four-chambered hearts with complete separation of pulmonary and systemic blood, supporting high metabolic activity.

questions.text: Why do we call our heart myogenic?
questions.answer: The human heart is myogenic because the impulse for contraction originates within the heart muscle, specifically at the sinoatrial (SA) node, rather than being initiated by a nerve.

questions.text: Sino-atrial node is called the pacemaker of our heart. Why?
questions.answer: The SA node spontaneously generates rhythmic electrical impulses at the highest rate in the heart, initiating each heartbeat and setting the pace for the rest of the cardiac conduction system.

questions.text: What is the significance of atrio-ventricular node and atrio-ventricular bundle in the functioning of heart?
questions.answer: The AV node receives the impulse from the atria and briefly delays it, allowing ventricles to fill. The AV bundle (bundle of His), bundle branches and Purkinje fibres conduct the impulse through ventricular myocardium for coordinated ventricular contraction.

questions.text: Define a cardiac cycle and the cardiac output.
questions.answer: A cardiac cycle is the sequence of atrial systole, ventricular systole and joint diastole during one heartbeat. Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute; at rest it is about 5 L/min (stroke volume × heart rate).

questions.text: Explain heart sounds.
questions.answer: The first heart sound, 'lub', is caused mainly by closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole. The second, 'dub', is caused by closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole.

questions.text: Draw a standard ECG and explain the different segments in it.
questions.answer: ECG: P wave = atrial depolarisation; QRS complex = ventricular depolarisation (atrial repolarisation is usually hidden within it); T wave = ventricular repolarisation. Draw baseline with labelled P, Q, R, S and T waves, PR interval and ST segment.

questions.text: Define Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR)
questions.answer: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute. In a healthy adult it is approximately 125 mL/min, or about 180 L/day.

questions.text: Explain the autoregulatory mechanism of GFR.
questions.answer: GFR is regulated by autoregulatory mechanisms that maintain relatively stable renal blood flow and filtration despite changes in arterial pressure. The myogenic response constricts/dilates afferent arterioles; tubuloglomerular feedback by the macula densa adjusts afferent arteriolar tone and renin release according to NaCl delivery.

questions.text: Indicate whether the following statements are true or false : (a) Micturition is carried out by a reflex. (b) ADH helps in water elimination, making the urine hypotonic. (c) Protein-free fluid is filtered from blood plasma into the Bowman’s capsule. (d) Henle’s loop plays an important role in concentrating the urine. (e) Glucose is actively reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False: ADH increases water reabsorption and makes urine more concentrated. (c) True: normal glomerular filtrate is essentially protein-free. (d) True. (e) True: glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT mainly by Na+-glucose cotransport.

questions.text: Give a brief account of the counter current mechanism.
questions.answer: The loop of Henle and vasa recta establish a counter-current system. Filtrate flows in opposite directions in descending and ascending limbs; the ascending limb transports NaCl out but is relatively impermeable to water, while the descending limb is permeable to water. This creates a medullary osmotic gradient, maintained by vasa recta, allowing collecting ducts to reabsorb water and concentrate urine.

questions.text: Describe the role of liver, lungs and skin in excretion.
questions.answer: The liver converts toxic ammonia to urea, metabolises haemoglobin into bile pigments and excretes cholesterol and some drugs in bile. Lungs remove CO2 and water vapour. Skin removes water, salts and small amounts of urea through sweat.

questions.text: Explain micturition.
questions.answer: Micturition is the process of expelling urine from the urinary bladder. Stretch receptors signal the spinal micturition centre when the bladder fills; parasympathetic impulses contract the detrusor muscle and relax the internal sphincter. Voluntary control of the external sphincter allows urination.

questions.text: Match the items of column I with those of column II : Column I Column II (a) Ammonotelism (i) Birds (b) Bowman’s capsule (ii) Water reabsorption (c) Micturition (iii) Bony fish (d) Uricotelism (iv) Urinary bladder (d) ADH (v) Renal tubule EXCRETORY PRODUCTS AND THEIR ELIMINATION 301
questions.answer: (a) Ammonotelism – (iii) bony fish; (b) Bowman's capsule – (v) renal tubule; (c) Micturition – (iv) urinary bladder; (d) Uricotelism – (i) birds; (e) ADH – (ii) water reabsorption.

questions.text: What is meant by the term osmoregulation?
questions.answer: Osmoregulation is the regulation of water and solute concentrations in body fluids to maintain osmotic balance and a stable internal environment.

questions.text: Terrestrial animals are generally either ureotelic or uricotelic, not ammonotelic, why ?
questions.answer: Ammonia is highly toxic and requires large amounts of water for dilution and excretion. Terrestrial animals conserve water, so they convert ammonia into less toxic urea or poorly soluble uric acid, which can be excreted with less water.

questions.text: What is the significance of juxta glomerular apparatus (JGA) in kidney function?
questions.answer: The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA), formed by juxtaglomerular cells and macula densa, senses changes in renal blood flow/NaCl delivery and releases renin. It helps regulate GFR and blood pressure through the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

questions.text: Name the following: (a) A chordate animal having flame cells as excretory structures (b) Cortical portions projecting between the medullary pyramids in the human kidney (c) A loop of capillary running parallel to the Henle’s loop.
questions.answer: (a) Amphioxus (Branchiostoma) is a chordate with protonephridia containing flame cells. (b) Renal columns (columns of Bertin). (c) Vasa recta.

questions.text: Fill in the gaps : (a) Ascending limb of Henle’s loop is _______ to water whereas the descending limb is _______ to it. (b) Reabsorption of water from distal parts of the tubules is facilitated by hormone _______. (c) Dialysis fluid contain all the constituents as in plasma except _______. (d) A healthy adult human excretes (on an average) _______ gm of urea/day.
questions.answer: (a) Ascending limb is impermeable to water; descending limb is permeable to water. (b) ADH (vasopressin). (c) Dialysis fluid lacks nitrogenous wastes (especially urea) and is formulated to have normal plasma concentrations of useful solutes. (d) About 25–30 g urea per day.

questions.text: Draw the diagram of a sarcomere of skeletal muscle showing different regions.
questions.answer: Draw a sarcomere between two Z-lines. Label Z-line, I-band, A-band, H-zone, M-line, thin actin filaments and thick myosin filaments. Thin filaments attach to Z-lines; thick filaments lie centrally.

questions.text: Define sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
questions.answer: The sliding filament theory states that muscle contraction occurs when thin actin filaments slide inward over thick myosin filaments, shortening the sarcomere without shortening the filaments themselves.

questions.text: Describe the important steps in muscle contraction. 314 BIOLOGY
questions.answer: Motor neuron releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction; the muscle membrane depolarises and the impulse travels along sarcolemma and T-tubules. Sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca2+, which binds troponin and shifts tropomyosin away from actin's binding sites. Myosin heads bind actin, perform power strokes using ATP, and pull actin inward. Repeated cross-bridge cycling shortens sarcomeres. Ca2+ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the muscle relaxes.

questions.text: Write true or false. If false change the statement so that it is true. (a) Actin is present in thin filament (b) H-zone of striated muscle fibre represents both thick and thin filaments. (c) Human skeleton has 206 bones. (d) There are 11 pairs of ribs in man. (e) Sternum is present on the ventral side of the body.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False: H-zone contains only thick myosin filaments. (c) True. (d) False: humans have 12 pairs of ribs. (e) True.

questions.text: Write the difference between : (a) Actin and Myosin (b) Red and White muscles (c) Pectoral and Pelvic girdle
questions.answer: (a) Actin forms thin filaments; myosin forms thick filaments and has projecting heads that bind actin and hydrolyse ATP. (b) Red muscles have much myoglobin, mitochondria and capillaries and resist fatigue; white muscles have less myoglobin and fatigue more quickly but can contract rapidly. (c) Pectoral girdle attaches forelimbs and is relatively light/mobile; pelvic girdle attaches hindlimbs, is strong and bears body weight.

questions.text: Match Column I with Column II : Column I Column II (a) Smooth muscle (i) Myoglobin (b) Tropomyosin (ii) Thin filament (c) Red muscle (iii) Sutures (d) Skull (iv) Involuntary
questions.answer: (a) Smooth muscle – (iv) involuntary; (b) Tropomyosin – (ii) thin filament; (c) Red muscle – (i) myoglobin; (d) Skull – (iii) sutures.

questions.text: What are the different types of movements exhibited by the cells of human body?
questions.answer: Human cells exhibit amoeboid movement (e.g. leucocytes), ciliary movement (e.g. ciliated epithelium of respiratory tract/oviduct) and muscular movement (skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscles).

questions.text: How do you distinguish between a skeletal muscle and a cardiac muscle?
questions.answer: Skeletal muscle is striated, voluntary, long cylindrical and multinucleate with peripheral nuclei; cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary, branched, usually has one central nucleus and intercalated discs, and contracts rhythmically.

questions.text: Name the type of joint between the following:- (a) atlas/axis (b) carpal/metacarpal of thumb (c) between phalanges (d) femur/acetabulum (e) between cranial bones (f) between pubic bones in the pelvic girdle
questions.answer: (a) Atlas/axis – pivot joint. (b) Carpal–metacarpal of thumb – saddle joint. (c) Between phalanges – hinge joint. (d) Femur/acetabulum – ball-and-socket joint. (e) Between cranial bones – fibrous suture (immovable). (f) Between pubic bones – cartilaginous symphysis.

questions.text: Fill in the blank spaces: (a) All mammals (except a few) have __________ cervical vertebra. (b) The number of phalanges in each limb of human is __________ (c) Thin filament of myofibril contains 2 ‘F’ actins and two other proteins namely __________ and __________. (d) In a muscle fibre Ca++ is stored in __________ (e) __________ and __________ pairs of ribs are called floating ribs. (f) The human cranium is made of __________ bones. NEURAL CONTROL AND COORDINATION 315
questions.answer: (a) Seven. (b) Fourteen phalanges in each hand/foot. (c) Tropomyosin and troponin. (d) Sarcoplasmic reticulum. (e) Eleventh and twelfth pairs. (f) Eight bones.

questions.text: Briefly describe the structure of the following: (a) Brain (b) Eye (c) Ear
questions.answer: (a) Brain: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain and hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla); protected by meninges and skull. (b) Eye: three coats—sclera/cornea, choroid/ciliary body/iris and retina; lens, aqueous humour and vitreous humour focus light on retina. (c) Ear: external ear (pinna, auditory canal), middle ear (tympanic membrane and ossicles) and inner ear (cochlea, vestibular apparatus and semicircular canals).

questions.text: Compare the following: (a) Central neural system (CNS) and Peripheral neural system (PNS) (b) Resting potential and action potential (c) Choroid and retina
questions.answer: (a) CNS consists of brain and spinal cord; PNS consists of cranial/spinal nerves and ganglia connecting CNS to body. (b) Resting potential is the polarised membrane state (inside negative); action potential is a rapid, temporary reversal of membrane potential caused by ion movement. (c) Choroid is a vascular, pigmented middle coat that nourishes the eye and absorbs stray light; retina is the light-sensitive inner layer containing rods and cones.

questions.text: Explain the following processes: (a) Polarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre (b) Depolarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre (c) Conduction of a nerve impulse along a nerve fibre (d) Transmission of a nerve impulse across a chemical synapse
questions.answer: (a) Polarisation: at rest, Na+/K+ pump and selective permeability maintain high Na+ outside and high K+ inside; inside is negative relative to outside. (b) Depolarisation: stimulus opens voltage-gated Na+ channels; Na+ enters and the inside becomes positive. (c) Local currents depolarise adjacent membrane, propagating the action potential along the axon; in myelinated fibres it jumps between nodes of Ranvier. (d) At a chemical synapse, an arriving impulse opens Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ triggers neurotransmitter release, which binds postsynaptic receptors and changes ion-channel activity.

questions.text: Draw labelled diagrams of the following: (a) Neuron (b) Brain (c) Eye (d) Ear
questions.answer: Neuron: label dendrites, cell body/cyton, nucleus, axon hillock, axon, myelin sheath, Schwann cell/neurilemma and nodes of Ranvier. Brain: label cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, cerebellum and medulla. Eye: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, ciliary body, retina, choroid, sclera, optic nerve, aqueous and vitreous humour. Ear: pinna, auditory canal, tympanum, malleus, incus, stapes, cochlea, semicircular canals and auditory nerve.

questions.text: Write short notes on the following: (a) Neural coordination (b) Forebrain (c) Midbrain (d) Hindbrain (e) Retina (f) Ear ossicles (g) Cochlea (h) Organ of Corti (i) Synapse
questions.answer: (a) Neural coordination: integration and control of body activities through neurons and neurotransmitters. (b) Forebrain: cerebrum for sensory perception, voluntary movement, memory and intelligence; thalamus relays sensory input; hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and endocrine/autonomic functions. (c) Midbrain: visual/auditory reflex centres and conduction pathways. (d) Hindbrain: pons relays signals, cerebellum coordinates posture/balance/movement, medulla controls vital autonomic functions. (e) Retina: rods for dim light, cones for colour and detail. (f) Ear ossicles: malleus, incus and stapes transmit/amplify tympanic vibrations. (g) Cochlea: spiral, fluid-filled hearing organ. (h) Organ of Corti: sensory organ on basilar membrane with hair cells. (i) Synapse: junction between neurons or neuron and effector.

questions.text: Give a brief account of: (a) Mechanism of synaptic transmission (b) Mechanism of vision (c) Mechanism of hearing
questions.answer: (a) Synaptic transmission: action potential → Ca2+ entry at presynaptic terminal → vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release → receptor binding postsynaptically → ion-channel change and postsynaptic response → transmitter removal. (b) Vision: light passes through cornea, pupil and lens to retina; photopigments in rods/cones change conformation, generating signals that pass through retinal neurons to optic nerve and visual cortex. (c) Hearing: sound vibrates tympanum and ossicles; stapes moves oval window, producing cochlear fluid waves; basilar membrane moves, bending hair-cell stereocilia in the organ of Corti; impulses travel via auditory nerve to brain.

questions.text: Answer briefly: (a) How do you perceive the colour of an object? (b) Which part of our body helps us in maintaining the body balance? (c) How does the eye regulate the amount of light that falls on the retina.
questions.answer: (a) Cones detect wavelengths of light; the brain compares signals from different cone types to perceive colour. (b) Vestibular apparatus of the inner ear (semicircular canals, utricle and saccule), with cerebellar integration, maintains balance. (c) Iris muscles change pupil diameter: circular muscles constrict it in bright light; radial muscles dilate it in dim light.

questions.text: Explain the following: (a) Role of Na+ in the generation of action potential. (b) Mechanism of generation of light-induced impulse in the retina. (c) Mechanism through which a sound produces a nerve impulse in the inner ear.
questions.answer: (a) Na+ influx through voltage-gated channels causes rapid depolarisation and the rising phase of an action potential. (b) Light changes retinal in photoreceptors, activating transducin and phosphodiesterase, lowering cGMP and closing cGMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels; the photoreceptor hyperpolarises and alters neurotransmitter release. (c) Cochlear hair-cell stereocilia bend with basilar membrane movement; mechanically gated channels open, hair cells depolarise, neurotransmitter is released and auditory nerve fibres fire.

questions.text: Differentiate between: (a) Myelinated and non-myelinated axons (b) Dendrites and axons (c) Rods and cones (d) Thalamus and Hypothalamus (e) Cerebrum and Cerebellum 330 BIOLOGY
questions.answer: (a) Myelinated axons have a myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier; impulses conduct rapidly by saltatory conduction. Non-myelinated axons lack this sheath and conduct continuously, more slowly. (b) Dendrites receive signals and conduct toward the cell body; axons conduct away from it. (c) Rods are sensitive in dim light and do not mediate colour; cones work in bright light and mediate colour/high acuity. (d) Thalamus relays sensory information; hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, autonomic and endocrine functions. (e) Cerebrum supports higher cognition and voluntary action; cerebellum coordinates movement, posture and balance.

questions.text: Answer the following: (a) Which part of the ear determines the pitch of a sound? (b) Which part of the human brain is the most developed? (c) Which part of our central neural system acts as a master clock?
questions.answer: (a) Basilar membrane/organ of Corti: different regions respond to different frequencies; high frequencies near the base and low frequencies near the apex, allowing pitch discrimination. (b) Cerebrum. (c) Suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.

questions.text: The region of the vertebrate eye, where the optic nerve passes out of the retina, is called the (a) fovea (b) iris (c) blind spot (d) optic chaisma
questions.answer: (c) Blind spot (optic disc).

questions.text: Distinguish between: (a) afferent neurons and efferent neurons (b) impulse conduction in a myelinated nerve fibre and unmyelinated nerve fibre (c) aqueous humor and vitreous humor (d) blind spot and yellow spot (f) cranial nerves and spinal nerves. CHEMICAL COORDINATION AND INTEGRATION 331
questions.answer: (a) Afferent neurons carry impulses from receptors to CNS; efferent neurons carry commands from CNS to effectors. (b) Myelinated fibres conduct by saltatory conduction between nodes and are faster; unmyelinated fibres conduct continuously and are slower. (c) Aqueous humour is watery fluid in the anterior eye chambers; vitreous humour is a gel filling the posterior cavity. (d) Blind spot lacks photoreceptors where optic nerve exits; yellow spot/fovea has dense cones and highest visual acuity. (f) Cranial nerves arise from brain (12 pairs); spinal nerves arise from spinal cord (31 pairs).

questions.text: Define the following: (a) Exocrine gland (b) Endocrine gland (c) Hormone
questions.answer: Exocrine gland: releases secretion through a duct onto a surface or into a cavity. Endocrine gland: ductless gland that releases hormones into blood/interstitial fluid. Hormone: a chemical messenger produced in small amounts by endocrine cells that regulates target cells with specific receptors.

questions.text: Diagrammatically indicate the location of the various endocrine glands in our body.
questions.answer: From head to trunk: pineal gland in brain; hypothalamus and pituitary at base of brain; thyroid in neck; parathyroids on posterior thyroid; thymus in upper chest; adrenal glands atop kidneys; pancreas in abdomen; testes in scrotum; ovaries in pelvic cavity. Also endocrine cells occur in heart, kidneys and gastrointestinal tract.

questions.text: List the hormones secreted by the following: (a) Hypothalamus (b) Pituitary (c) Thyroid (d) Parathyroid (e) Adrenal (f) Pancreas (g) Testis (h) Ovary (i) Thymus (j) Atrium (k) Kidney (l) G-I Tract
questions.answer: (a) Hypothalamus: releasing and inhibiting hormones (e.g. GnRH, TRH, CRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine); also synthesises ADH and oxytocin. (b) Pituitary: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, MSH; posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin. (c) Thyroid: T4, T3, calcitonin. (d) Parathyroid: PTH. (e) Adrenal: cortex—cortisol, aldosterone, adrenal androgens; medulla—adrenaline and noradrenaline. (f) Pancreas: insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, pancreatic polypeptide. (g) Testis: testosterone and inhibin. (h) Ovary: estrogens, progesterone, inhibin, relaxin. (i) Thymus: thymosins. (j) Atrium: atrial natriuretic factor/peptide (ANF/ANP). (k) Kidney: erythropoietin, renin, calcitriol. (l) G-I tract: gastrin, secretin, CCK, GIP, motilin and related gut peptides.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks: Hormones Target gland (a) Hypothalamic hormones __________________ (b) Thyrotrophin (TSH) __________________ (c) Corticotrophin (ACTH) __________________ (d) Gonadotrophins (LH, FSH) __________________ (e) Melanotrophin (MSH) __________________
questions.answer: (a) Hypothalamic hormones → anterior pituitary. (b) TSH → thyroid gland. (c) ACTH → adrenal cortex. (d) LH and FSH → gonads (ovaries/testes). (e) MSH → melanocytes/pigment cells.

questions.text: Write short notes on the functions of the following hormones: (a) Parathyroid hormone (PTH) (b) Thyroid hormones (c) Thymosins (d) Androgens (e) Estrogens (f) Insulin and Glucagon
questions.answer: (a) PTH raises blood Ca2+ by promoting bone resorption, renal Ca2+ reabsorption and activation of vitamin D; it lowers phosphate reabsorption. (b) Thyroid hormones increase basal metabolic rate and support growth/development; calcitonin lowers blood Ca2+. (c) Thymosins promote T-lymphocyte development and immunity. (d) Androgens promote male reproductive organ development, spermatogenesis and secondary sexual characters. (e) Estrogens promote female reproductive organ development, secondary sexual characters and endometrial growth. (f) Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake/storage; glucagon raises it by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.text: Give example(s) of: (a) Hyperglycemic hormone and hypoglycemic hormone (b) Hypercalcemic hormone (c) Gonadotrophic hormones (d) Progestational hormone (e) Blood pressure lowering hormone (f) Androgens and estrogens
questions.answer: (a) Hyperglycemic: glucagon; hypoglycemic: insulin. (b) PTH. (c) FSH and LH. (d) Progesterone. (e) ANF/ANP. (f) Androgens: testosterone; estrogens: estradiol.

questions.text: Which hormonal deficiency is responsible for the following: (a) Diabetes mellitus (b) Goitre (c) Cretinism
questions.answer: (a) Diabetes mellitus: insulin deficiency or ineffective insulin action (classically insulin deficiency in the NCERT context). (b) Goitre: commonly iodine deficiency causing reduced thyroid hormone synthesis and thyroid enlargement. (c) Cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism): deficiency of thyroid hormones during early development.

questions.text: Briefly mention the mechanism of action of FSH.
questions.answer: FSH binds to specific receptors on target cells (granulosa cells in ovarian follicles and Sertoli cells in testes). It activates intracellular signalling, commonly via cAMP, promoting follicular development and estrogen secretion in females and supporting spermatogenesis in males.

questions.text: Match the following: Column I Column II (a) T4 (i) Hypothalamus (b) PTH (ii) Thyroid (c) GnRH (iii) Pituitary (d) LH (iv) Parathyroid NOTE CHEMICAL COORDINATION AND INTEGRATION 345 NOTE NOTE
questions.answer: Matching: (a) T4 – (ii) Thyroid; (b) PTH – (iv) Parathyroid; (c) GnRH – (i) Hypothalamus; (d) LH – (iii) Pituitary.
